questions.question: A hundred chart shows the numbers 1 to 100 written in 10 rows of 10. Ava shades every number she lands on when she skip-counts by 3, and she stops after 8 shaded numbers: 3, 6, 9, 12, 15, 18, 21, 24. So 3 × 8 = 24. Ava now doubles to work out 6 × 8. What is 6 × 8?
questions.explain: Because 6 is double 3, the product doubles too: 24 + 24 = 48. The usual trap is adding one more group (24 + 8 = 32) instead of doubling the whole product.

questions.question: On a hundred chart (the numbers 1 to 100 in 10 rows of 10), Ben shades every number he lands on when he skip-counts by 10, stopping after 7 shaded numbers: 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70. So 10 × 7 = 70. Ben now halves to work out 5 × 7. What is 5 × 7?
questions.explain: Since 5 is half of 10, the product is halved: half of 70 is 35. A common slip is subtracting 5 or 10 from 70 instead of halving it.

questions.question: On a hundred chart with the numbers 1 to 100 in 10 rows of 10, Priya shades every number she lands on skip-counting by 2, stopping after 7 shaded numbers: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14. So 2 × 7 = 14. Priya doubles once to get 4 × 7, then doubles again to get 8 × 7. What is 8 × 7?
questions.explain: Double twice: 14 doubles to 28 (that is 4 × 7), and 28 doubles to 56 (that is 8 × 7). Many children stop after one double and answer 28, or add 14 instead of doubling the second time.

questions.question: On a hundred chart (numbers 1 to 100, in 10 rows of 10), Owen shades every number he lands on skip-counting by 4, stopping after 6 shaded numbers: 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, 24. So 4 × 6 = 24. Owen now halves to find 2 × 6. What is 2 × 6?
questions.explain: Halving the factor 4 to make 2 halves the product as well: half of 24 is 12. Watch the direction — going from 4 groups down to 2 groups means halving, not doubling.

questions.question: Ella knows that 3 × 7 = 21. Which is the correct way to use doubling to find 6 × 7?
options: Double 21, because 6 is double 3 — the answer is 42
Double 21 and double 7 — the answer is 84
Add 7 to 21, because 6 is bigger than 3 — the answer is 28
questions.explain: When one factor doubles, the product doubles: 21 + 21 = 42. The trap is doubling the other factor as well, which makes the answer far too big.

questions.question: Halving one factor and doubling the other keeps the answer the same. Which of these has the same answer as 16 × 5?
questions.explain: Halve 16 to 8 and double 5 to 10: 8 × 10 = 80, the same as 16 × 5. If you double one factor without halving the other, the answer doubles instead of staying the same.

questions.question: At a Burnaby library, books are packed in boxes of 8. Owen knows that 5 boxes hold 40 books. He uses doubling to work out how many books are in 10 boxes. How many books is that?
questions.explain: Since 10 boxes is double 5 boxes, double the product: 40 + 40 = 80. Adding just one more box (40 + 8 = 48) is the usual mistake — doubling means adding another five boxes, not another one.

questions.question: Nadia knows that 8 × 7 = 56. She halves the factor 8 and halves the product. Which true fact does this give her?
questions.explain: Half of 8 is 4 and half of 56 is 28, so 4 × 7 = 28. Only the one factor gets halved — the 7 stays the same, and halving does not mean subtracting 4 from 56.

questions.question: Jasmin knows that 4 × 6 = 24. She wants to find 8 × 12, so she says: 8 is double 4 and 12 is double 6, so I just double 24. She writes 48. What is 8 × 12 really?
questions.explain: Doubling one factor doubles the product, so 8 × 6 = 48, and doubling the second factor doubles it again: 8 × 12 = 96. This is the most common trap — when both factors double, the product needs doubling twice, not once.

questions.question: At a Kelowna community centre, each table seats 6 people. On Monday 5 tables are set up. On Tuesday the number of tables is doubled. How many people can be seated on Monday and Tuesday altogether?
questions.explain: Monday is 5 × 6 = 30; Tuesday has double the tables, so double the seats, 60; together that is 30 + 60 = 90. Answering 60 forgets Monday, and adding one extra table (30 + 6 = 36) is not doubling.

questions.question: A pack of 4 granola bars costs $3 at a Victoria store. Mateo buys 8 packs for a school hike. He works it out by doubling: 4 packs cost 4 × $3 = $12, and 8 packs is double 4 packs. How much do the 8 packs cost?
questions.explain: Doubling the number of packs doubles the cost: $12 + $12 = $24. The trap is answering $32, which is the number of granola bars (8 × 4), not the money.

questions.question: Noah knows that 6 × 8 = 48. To find 3 × 8 he halves the 6 to get 3 and also halves the 8 to get 4, then answers 12. What is 3 × 8, and what went wrong?
options: 12 — halving both the 6 and the 8 was the right move, since 3 × 4 is half of 6 × 8
40 — take 8 away from 48, because 3 × 8 is just one group of 8 less than 6 × 8
48 — halving a factor does not change the product, so 3 × 8 is the same as 6 × 8
24 — only the 6 should be halved, so the product halves once: half of 48 is 24
questions.explain: Halve one factor and the product halves, so 3 × 8 = half of 48 = 24. Halving both factors halves the answer twice, which is why Noah landed on 12.
